Drop a pebble into a still pond. A ring of ripples spreads out from the splash. A leaf floating inside the ring has already bobbed; a leaf further out sits perfectly still, and nothing about that splash can reach it until the ripple arrives.

Light behaves like those ripples, and it gives us the second barrier on the road to the past.

---

Picture a single event: a flash at one spot, at one instant [16]. Its light races outward in every direction [16]. Pretend space is a flat tabletop and the light spreads as a growing circle [16]. Now stack those circles one on top of another, one for each moment, with time running upward. The stack makes a cone, and physicists call it the future light cone of that event [16].

The cone matters because of a speed limit. Light in empty space travels at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, about a billion kilometres per hour [17]. That number is so fixed that the metre itself is now defined by how far light goes in a sliver of a second [17]. According to special relativity nothing can go faster than light, and only massless particles such as photons, the particles of light, can go that fast at all [15].

So the light cone is a map of influence. An event can only affect what lies on or inside its future light cone [16]. Anything outside the cones on both sides is cut off: the two events can neither see nor touch each other [16]. This is causality, the rule that a cause comes before its effect. You flick the switch, and only then does the lamp flood the room. The cone keeps that order intact.

---

Now ask what it would take to break the rule. Physicists have dreamed up particles called tachyons that would always outrun light [15]. If they existed, they would break causality and open the door to time travel [15]. The scientific consensus, though, is that they don't exist, and every scrap of matter anyone has observed moves slower than light [15].

That's the heart of it. To send anything into the past you would have to step outside the cone, and nothing we've ever watched does that. Which leaves a fair question hanging: if you somehow managed it, what would go wrong? The answer comes as a famous set of puzzles.
